plan.contextChunk: This figure is a single labeled diagram of an upward-opening parabola drawn on a Cartesian coordinate plane, with thin black arrowed axes crossing near the lower left of the curve and marked x at the right and y at the top. The parabola is a heavy dark blue curve whose two branches end in arrowheads pointing up and outward. Its lowest point is a filled dark blue dot above the horizontal x-axis, connected by a short leader line to the label Vertex at the left. A dashed orange vertical line rises through that dot and carries the orange label Axis of symmetry at the upper right. Directly above the vertex on that same vertical line sits a small teal dot labeled Focus in teal. A short dashed blue horizontal segment runs through the teal dot from one branch of the curve to the other and is tagged Latus rectum by a curved arrow from the upper left. Below the vertex, a dashed red horizontal line spanning the width of the frame is labeled Directrix in red, and the x-axis lies lower in the frame. Color-coding the four named features separately lets the reader see that the axis of symmetry meets the directrix at a right angle and that the vertex lies midway between focus and directrix. The drawing establishes the vocabulary used to define a parabola as the set of points equally distant from the focus and the directrix.

demo_steps.title: Name the parts of the parabola
demo_steps.narration: Start with the labeled feature view. The focus lies above the vertex, the directrix lies the same distance below it, and the orange axis of symmetry passes through both the focus and vertex at a right angle to the directrix.

demo_steps.title: Change p and watch the shape respond
demo_steps.narration: Increase p: the focus rises, the directrix mirrors downward, and the parabola opens wider. Decrease p: the focus and directrix move closer to the vertex, producing a narrower curve.

demo_steps.title: Reveal the equal-distance rule
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the distance construction view. A point on the parabola is connected to the focus and to the directrix by a perpendicular segment, showing the two distances are equal.

demo_steps.title: See why the vertex is halfway
demo_steps.narration: At the vertex, the distance upward to the focus equals the distance downward to the directrix. That midpoint relationship explains why the vertex sits exactly between them.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The parabola's shape is completely controlled by the equal-distance relationship to a focus and a directrix, with the vertex exactly halfway between them.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Use a clean Cartesian coordinate plane with black arrowed axes crossing left of the parabola's center and below the vertex. Draw the parabola as a thick dark blue upward-opening curve with arrowheads at the upper ends. Place the vertex on the orange dashed vertical axis, above the x-axis; place the teal focus directly above the vertex and the red dashed directrix the same distance below it. Keep the axis of symmetry orange, directrix red, focus teal, and parabola/latus rectum blue to match the original visual coding. In labeled view, show the labels Vertex, Focus, Directrix, Axis of symmetry, and Latus rectum with leader lines. In distance construction view, fade most labels and emphasize a sample point on the curve, its segment to the focus, and its perpendicular segment to the directrix with equal-distance markings.

authoredContext:
In Quadratic Functions, we learned about a parabola’s vertex and axis of symmetry. Now we extend the discussion to include other key features of the parabola. See the figure. Notice that the axis of symmetry passes through the focus and vertex and is perpendicular to the directrix. The vertex is the midpoint between the directrix and the focus.

The line segment that passes through the focus and is parallel to the directrix is called the latus rectum. The endpoints of the latus rectum lie on the curve. By definition, the distance d from the focus to any point P on the parabola is equal to the distance from P to the directrix.

Key features of the parabola

This image displays a parabola on a Cartesian coordinate plane, clearly labeling its fundamental geometric elements. The blue curve represents the parabola itself. The "Vertex" is indicated as the turning point of the parabola. Inside the curve, the "Focus" is marked, a critical point for defining the parabola. A dashed orange line, labeled "Axis of symmetry", passes vertically through both the vertex and the focus. Below the vertex, a horizontal dashed red line shows the "Directrix". Finally, a horizontal dashed blue line segment passing through the focus and extending to the parabola is identified as the "Latus rectum".

To work with parabolas in the coordinate plane, we consider two cases: those with a vertex at the origin and those with a vertex at a point other than the origin. We begin with the former.

discrepancies: the parabola branch arrowheads are oversized filled triangular markers, whereas the source uses small simple arrowheads integrated with the curve strokes
the directrix label sits directly on the dashed red directrix line instead of being placed clearly above it as in the source
the focus label overlaps the blue latus-rectum guide line more than in the source, reducing clarity around the focus point
the generated latus rectum is drawn as a full dashed horizontal construction line through the focus, while the source shows it more subtly with the label leader emphasizing the segment near the focus
the default composition is noticeably wider and more spread out, with the curve and annotations occupying a different balance relative to the axes than the compact source figure
evaluation.notes: The generated figure captures the main parabola, focus, vertex, directrix, axis of symmetry, and latus rectum accurately, but oversized curve arrowheads and a few label-placement/proportion issues keep it from being a clean drop-in match.
action_items: Reduce the parabola arrowhead marker size substantially and use a slimmer arrowhead style closer to the source.
Move the Directrix label slightly above the dashed red line so the text does not sit on top of the line.
Shift the Focus label up or right so it does not collide with the dashed latus-rectum line.
Tune the scale and horizontal spacing so the curve, axes, and annotations match the more compact proportions of the source figure.
